genZNote: Classified as a fungus by molecular phylogenetics but still can't be grown in a dish — diagnosis means looking directly at the lung sample.

morphology.shape: Trophic forms (thin-walled, amoeboid) and cystic forms (thick-walled, cup-shaped/crushed-ping-pong-ball appearance)
morphology.size: Cysts ~4-6 µm diameter, each containing up to 8 intracystic bodies

reproductiveStructures: Cystic form with up to 8 intracystic bodies

habitat.naturalHabitat: Human and mammalian lung alveoli — tightly host-adapted with species-specific strains across different mammals
habitat.hostAssociation: Likely acquired via airborne transmission early in life in most people, then remains latent/controlled by an intact immune system; reactivates or causes progressive disease when cell-mediated immunity is impaired
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Not established as free-living in the environment — appears to require an animal host
habitat.reservoir: Human lungs (person-to-person airborne transmission is increasingly recognized, particularly among immunocompromised contacts)

microscopy.stain: Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain, toluidine blue O, or direct fluorescent antibody staining of bronchoalveolar lavage/induced sputum
microscopy.appearance: Cup-shaped or crushed-ping-pong-ball-shaped cysts on GMS stain

culture.media: Not applicable — cannot be cultured on artificial media using standard clinical laboratory techniques
culture.growthCharacteristics: No in vitro culture system is available for routine clinical diagnosis

biochemicalTests.result: Often markedly elevated in Pneumocystis pneumonia (nonspecific but supportive)
Highly sensitive, increasingly used for diagnosis

identificationClues: Cannot be cultured — diagnosis requires direct visualization (GMS/toluidine blue stain) or PCR of bronchoalveolar lavage or induced sputum
Classic cup-shaped or crushed-ping-pong-ball cysts on Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain
Bilateral, diffuse ground-glass opacities on chest CT in a patient with hypoxia disproportionate to chest X-ray findings
Strongly associated with CD4 count <200 cells/µL in HIV/AIDS patients, or other significant cell-mediated immunosuppression

diseases: Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP/PJP) — subacute fever, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea with bilateral interstitial/ground-glass infiltrates; a classic AIDS-defining illness
virulenceFactors: Tight attachment to type I alveolar pneumocytes, disrupting gas exchange
Ability to persist in a low-immunity host without triggering an overwhelming acute inflammatory response until late in disease
clinicalImportance.transmission: Airborne, person-to-person, likely with most people acquiring subclinical infection in early childhood; disease results from either reactivation or new infection in the setting of impaired cell-mediated immunity
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: A leading cause of opportunistic pneumonia in patients with HIV/AIDS (particularly CD4 <200 cells/µL) and other causes of significant T-cell immunosuppression (e.g., organ transplant, prolonged high-dose corticosteroids); trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis is standard in high-risk patients
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Because it cannot be cultured, clinical suspicion combined with imaging, an elevated serum (1→3)-β-D-glucan, and direct staining or PCR of respiratory specimens together drive the diagnosis

examFacts.shape: Cup-shaped cysts with intracystic bodies; trophic forms
examFacts.importantDisease: Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) — classic AIDS-defining opportunistic infection
examFacts.importantTest: GMS stain of bronchoalveolar lavage; serum (1→3)-β-D-glucan; PCR
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: An opportunistic fungus that cannot be cultured and causes AIDS-defining pneumonia, diagnosed by direct staining of respiratory specimens rather than culture
